title: Tests with assert
summary: Write pytest-style tests: plain functions and plain asserts.

steps.title: assert
body: `assert condition, "message"` raises `AssertionError` if the condition is false:
**pytest**, the standard Python test runner, builds on this. A test is just a function whose name starts with `test_`, in a file named `test_*.py`. No classes, no attributes, no `Assert.AreEqual`:
Run `pytest` in the project folder and it finds and runs them all. When an assert fails, pytest shows both sides of the comparison.

steps.prompt: Which of these would pytest collect and run as a test?
steps.explain: By default pytest looks for files named `test_*.py` (or `*_test.py`) and functions named `test_*`.

steps.title: Testing for exceptions
body: `match=` is a regex searched in the exception's message, so the test also proves it failed for the right reason.

Earlier steps in this lesson test by hand, with plain functions. From the last step on, the dojo runs **real pytest** (`python -m pytest`): your test file is collected and run exactly as it would be on your machine or in CI, and its output is shown. Outside the dojo, install it per project: `uv add --dev pytest` (or `python -m pip install pytest` inside a virtual environment).

steps.title: Test a slugify function
prompt: Someone else is writing `slugify(text)`: it lowercases, trims, replaces runs of spaces with a single `-`, and removes every character that is not a letter, digit or `-`.

**You write only the tests**: at least three `test_` functions with `assert`. **Run checks** runs them against a correct `slugify` and against several broken ones; good tests pass on the first and fail on each broken one.
template: for dojo_n, dojo_f in sorted((k, v) for k, v in globals().items() if k.startswith('test_') and callable(v)):
dojo_count = len([k for k in list(globals()) if k.startswith('test_')])
Dojo.check('you wrote at least 3 test_ functions', dojo_count >= 3, f'found {dojo_count}')
Dojo.check('all your tests pass on a correct slugify', not dojo_failed, 'failing: ' + ', '.join(dojo_failed))
Dojo.check('your tests catch the bug: does not trim', bool(dojo_run_tests()), 'every test still passed on this broken version')
Dojo.check('your tests catch the bug: keeps punctuation', bool(dojo_run_tests()), 'every test still passed on this broken version')
Dojo.check('your tests catch the bug: one dash per space', bool(dojo_run_tests()), 'every test still passed on this broken version')
hints: Test each rule separately: one test per behaviour, named after it.
Cover trimming (`"  x "`), several spaces in a row, and punctuation.
Be careful with `"C# & .NET!"`: after removing symbols there are dashes on both sides of `&`; the correct result is `c-net`.

steps.title: Real pytest: does your suite catch the bugs?
prompt: slugify("Ünïcode")         # "n-code": anything outside a-z and 0-9 becomes a dash

Write a pytest file for it (`from slugify import slugify`). **Run checks** runs it with real pytest against the correct code, then against four broken copies (a planted bug in each). A good suite passes on the first and fails on every broken one.
Use `@pytest.mark.parametrize` for the normal cases and `pytest.raises` for the empty title. At least 4 tests (each parametrize case counts).

mutants.name: leading and trailing dashes are kept
mutants.hint: Try a title that starts or ends with spaces or punctuation.

mutants.name: runs of punctuation become several dashes
mutants.hint: Try `"Hello, World!"`: comma plus space is two characters.

hints: One parametrized test with pairs `(title, expected)`, one test for the blank title.
Each planted bug needs an input that shows it: capitals, a leading space, `", "` between words, and `"   "`.
steps.explain: This is mutation testing in miniature: a test suite is only as good as the bugs it catches. Coverage would call `test_simple` alone 100%, yet it misses three of the four bugs.
